conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers sort through the emotional ups and downs that can come after a baby arrives. I’ll be guiding you through a quick screening tool that many mothers find helpful. It’s called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—and it simply gives us a snapshot of how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days so we can make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

Everything we discuss stays confidential within our care team, and there’s no right or wrong answer—just your honest experience. We’ll take about two minutes to go through 10 gentle questions. If any question feels hard to talk about, we can slow down or pause. My goal is to keep you and your baby safe and emotionally well.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?
Honestly... it’s been hard. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday and I tried to laugh, but it felt kind of forced. I used to laugh at everything—now it’s like the joy is behind a pane of glass.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I mean, I *can* laugh, but it feels kind of hollow. Mostly I’m just too tired or worried to find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much lately. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like another chore. I still try to plan stuff, but I’m kind of going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right. Last night he wouldn’t settle for two hours and I kept replaying everything—did I eat something that bothered him, am I holding him wrong, am I just a lousy mom? My head knows babies cry, but it still feels like my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s not breathing right, or I’ll imagine him rolling off the couch even though he’s strapped in. Nothing sets it off—my mind just jumps to the worst. I can usually talk myself down, but it keeps coming back.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

It’s happened a few times this week. Like yesterday—I was folding laundry while the baby napped and suddenly my chest got tight, heart pounding, this wave of “something awful is about to happen.” No warning, no reason. I had to sit on the floor and breathe through it. It passed after a couple of minutes, but it left me shaky the rest of the afternoon.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days. Between the feeding, the diapers, the pumping, the laundry, trying to sleep in 90-minute chunks, plus remembering to eat—there’s this constant weight on my chest. Some mornings I open my eyes and already feel behind. I keep telling myself “just get through the next hour,” but the pile never shrinks.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

A few nights this week I couldn’t fall asleep even when the baby was out. I’d lie there listening to every squeak from the bassinet, running through everything I might have messed up, feeling this heavy sadness in my chest. I finally drift off, but then I’m wide awake the second he stirs.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… that’s been my baseline lately. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a gray cloud hanging over everything. Even when the baby smiles—those sweet little gummy grins—I feel this ache instead of joy. Yesterday I just sat in the rocker with him and cried for no clear reason.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Pretty much every day this week. Sometimes it’s just tears leaking while I’m nursing, other times it’s full-on sobbing after I put him down. Yesterday I cried because I couldn’t get the stroller unfolded—something that used to be simple. The littlest thing sets me off, and once I start it’s hard to stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself. I just want to feel like me again—for my baby’s sake as much as mine.

You've painted a clear picture of how heavy life has felt since your baby arrived. Despite your best efforts, joy seems distant, everyday tasks feel like uphill battles, and waves of worry or sadness crash over you most days. You're exhausted yet vigilant, crying easily, and blaming yourself whenever anything feels off, even though part of you knows you're doing your best. Hearing how you described the "gray cloud" that follows you and the "hollow" laughter shows just how real and draining these feelings are.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient indicates a clear reduction in ability to enjoy humor; "hollow" laughter and being "too tired or worried" aligns with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment compared to before, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame ('a lot') tied to specific incidents and global self-labeling ('lousy mom'), aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, intrusive worries occurring "pretty much every day" without a clear trigger, matching the highest severity.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic episodes occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days" with a "constant weight" and inability to reduce the burden, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple nights of difficulty falling and staying asleep directly linked to unhappiness and intrusive worries, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness ('baseline'), waking heavy, inability to feel joy at baby's smiles, and unexplained crying—aligns with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time".</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS score of 24 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating a high probability of <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You meet core <med>DSM-5</med> criteria: depressed mood most of the day, diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/guilt, fatigue, and recurrent thoughts of inadequacy. <sym>Anxiety symptoms</sym> and <sym>panic attacks</sym> are also prominent. You denied self-harm thoughts, so immediate safety risk is lower, but symptom severity and functional impairment warrant urgent evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to discuss diagnosis and treatment options such as <med>evidence-based therapy</med> and, if appropriate, <med>antidepressant medication</med> safe for breastfeeding
2. Plan daily 15-30 minutes of protected rest or pleasurable activity (e.g., music, short walk) while a partner, family member, or friend cares for the baby; small breaks can ease the sense of overwhelm
3. Practice good-enough parenting: lower housekeeping standards, accept help with chores, and remind yourself babies cry-this does not mean you are failing
4. Keep a simple log of mood, sleep hours, and any <sym>panic episodes</sym> to review with your clinician; noting patterns can guide treatment
5. Reach out to local or online <med>postpartum support groups</med> and national resources like Postpartum Support International for peer understanding and encouragement
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤12 wks post-delivery. Source: self-report via EPDS-style questionnaire.

Symptoms endorsed (frequency: daily–near daily)  
- Persistent low mood, “gray cloud,” crying spells  
- Marked anhedonia; activities feel like “chores”  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt re parenting competence  
- Generalized anxiety, catastrophic worries about infant safety  
- Discrete panic episodes (physical symptoms, no clear trigger)  
- Overwhelm, feeling “behind,” tasks “piling”  
- Initial insomnia and restless/hypervigilant sleep even when infant sleeps  

Safety  
- Denies self-harm or suicidal ideation (endorsed item 10=0)  
- No current protective service concerns

Pattern  
Consistent with moderate-severe depressive and anxiety symptoms in postpartum context; impairment in sleep, mood regulation, and daily functioning.

Screening significance  
High likelihood Edinburgh score ≥12; meets threshold for further evaluation for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety. Recommend expedited referral to reproductive psychiatry / perinatal mental health for comprehensive assessment and discussion of evidence-based treatment options.
